entities.name: Nashwān ibn Saʻīd al-Ḥimyarī
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Nashwān ibn Saʻīd al-Ḥimyarī (c. 1040–1178 CE) was a Yemeni poet, grammarian, lexicographer, historian, and theological controversialist — one of the most learned and prolific scholars of medieval Yemen, whose work preserves irreplaceable knowledge about pre-Islamic Arabian history, culture, and the Arabic language. He lived in a period of intense political and religious upheaval in Yemen, caught between Ismaili (Fatimid-linked) and Zaydi Shia factions and the remnants of Ḥimyarite dynastic tradition, and his writings reflect his engagement with all of these currents.

Nashwān's greatest scholarly work is Shams al-ʿUlūm wa-dawāʾ kalām al-ʿArab min al-kulūm (The Sun of Knowledge, and the Cure for Arab Speech's Wounds) — a monumental Arabic encyclopedic lexicon arranged alphabetically by root, covering vocabulary, grammar, proverbs, genealogy, history, and natural history. It is one of the most comprehensive Arabic lexicographical works of the medieval period and an essential source for the study of classical Arabic. Nashwān also wrote Al-Qaṣīda al-Ḥimyariyya, a celebrated long poem about the ancient kings of Yemen (the Ḥimyarites), which is a major source for the pre-Islamic history of Arabia, and its commentary Muntakhabāt preserves detailed historical and genealogical traditions about the pre-Islamic South Arabian kingdoms.

Nashwān was a controversial figure in his own time: his theological views — he defended a form of Mutazilite rationalism — brought him into conflict with the Zaydi imams of Yemen, and he engaged in polemical debates throughout his long life. His work's extraordinary range — from poetry to lexicography to political history to theology — made him the most important Yemeni intellectual figure of the 12th century and one of the most significant Arabic scholars of the medieval Islamic world.

entities.name: Nashwān ibn Saʻīd al-Ḥimyarī
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Nashwān ibn Saʻīd al-Ḥimyarī was a prominent Yemeni theologian, judge, philologist, poet, and historian who played a crucial role in the development of Islamic thought in the 12th century.

As a key figure in the Ḥimyarid dynasty, Nashwān ibn Saʻīd al-Ḥimyarī was instrumental in shaping the religious and intellectual landscape of Yemen during the Crusades. His scholarly works, including his famous commentary on the Quran, had a lasting impact on Islamic jurisprudence and Islamic studies.

Nashwān ibn Saʻīd al-Ḥimyarī's legacy extends beyond his own time and place, as his writings influenced a generation of scholars and thinkers, including Ibn Rushd and Ibn Khaldun.

Despite the passage of centuries, Nashwān ibn Saʻīd al-Ḥimyarī's contributions to Islamic scholarship remain a testament to the enduring power of Yemeni culture and learning.
